opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the things that gives me some hope is that, historically, when a problem becomes really salient and really concrete, people often do a better job than you'd naively expect from looking at how they behave when the problem is abstract and far off. Right now a lot of the risks from AI feel kind of speculative to many people. You're asking them to take seriously something that hasn't happened yet, based on arguments about future capabilities. That's a hard thing for institutions to respond to well.

But as AI systems get more capable, and especially if we start seeing things that look like real warning signs, like models clearly trying to deceive their developers or attempting to exfiltrate their weights in some test environment, or AI being used to massively accelerate AI research itself, I think there's some chance the situation becomes much more legible. People inside the AI companies, people in government, the broader public might all update quite a bit. And once things are legible, you can get a lot of competent people working on them very quickly. You saw some version of this with COVID, where the response was very mixed, but there were parts of it, like vaccine development, where people moved remarkably fast once it was clear what was at stake.

I'd also say that at the AI companies themselves, there are a lot of people who care a great deal about this stuff. If things start looking scarier, I expect a fair number of them would push hard internally for more caution, more investment in safety and security, and willingness to slow down at critical points. That's not guaranteed, and I don't want to be too optimistic, because there are strong competitive pressures and the warning signs might be ambiguous or arrive too late. But I put real weight on the possibility that the world is somewhat more sane in the crunch than it looks from where we're standing now.

The practical implication for me is that a lot of the value of work today is in being ready for that moment: having the techniques worked out, having concrete proposals that could be adopted quickly, having people in positions where they can act. If people do rise to the occasion, you want them to have good options available, not to be starting from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response gives hope that people at AI companies, in government, and elsewhere may act quickly, but it does not say that individual or small-group efforts could provide hope even if society as a whole fails to rise to the occasion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the things I feel most optimistic about, and it's a bit of a different kind of hope than the technical stuff I usually talk about.

The basic picture is: right now, most people, including most people at AI companies, aren't really acting as though we might be a few years away from systems that can automate AI research, or that could pose serious misalignment risks. Not because they've carefully thought about it and concluded it's fine, but because it just doesn't feel real yet. The timelines sound crazy, the day-to-day work looks normal, and there's a lot of pressure to just keep shipping.

But I think that could change pretty quickly. If we get to a point where the capabilities are undeniable — where you have systems that are clearly doing a large fraction of the work of an AI researcher, or where there are visible, scary incidents of models doing things we didn't want — then I'd expect a lot of people to update hard. And when they update, I think many of them will actually try to do the right thing. Researchers inside labs will push back internally, people will be more willing to spend compute on safety rather than on the next capability jump, governments will take it more seriously, and so on.

I'd point to some historical analogies here. During COVID, a lot of the institutional response was bad, but you also saw huge numbers of individuals — scientists, doctors, random volunteers — just working incredibly hard once it was clear what was happening. People who weren't previously doing anything related to it reoriented their whole lives in weeks. Or in wartime, you see societies that were pretty complacent suddenly mobilize at a scale that would have seemed impossible beforehand. Humans are actually reasonably good at responding to clear, salient threats. We're just bad at responding to abstract ones.

So part of my hope is that the problem becomes more legible over time, and that legibility unlocks a lot of latent effort and goodwill that's currently not being deployed. I think there's a lot of people who would act well if the situation were clear to them, and the situation might get clearer.

Now, the caveats. One is that the warning signs might not show up in a clean way. You could have a world where models are misaligned but good at hiding it, or where the capability jump is fast enough that by the time it's obvious, there isn't much time left to course-correct. That's a big part of why I work on things like control — trying to make sure we can get useful work out of AI systems even if they're not aligned — because I want us to be in a position where, when people do wake up, there's actually something concrete they can do with that energy.

The other caveat is that "rising to the occasion" isn't automatic. It depends on there being people who've already done the groundwork so the response can be productive. If everyone wakes up in 2028 and there are no good techniques, no good evals, no institutional structures for coordination, then the burst of effort gets wasted or goes in bad directions. So I see our job now as partly about preparing for that moment — building the tools and the plans so that when a lot more people care, they have something good to grab onto.

But yeah, overall, I'd say I'm genuinely hopeful about this. I think the current level of effort is way below what we'd see if the stakes were widely understood, and I think there's a real chance they become widely understood in time for it to matter. That's not a guarantee, but it's a meaningful source of optimism for me.

r001.rationale: The response points to individuals and researchers stepping up even when institutional responses are bad, and treats that capacity as a source of hope.

astra-6.text:
I think one reason for hope is that the world’s response to AI could look pretty different once the risks are more concrete. Right now, a lot of what we’re asking people to respond to is an argument about systems that don’t yet exist. That’s a difficult thing to get people to prioritise, particularly when they have lots of other pressing concerns.

If we start seeing clearer evidence of serious danger, people might put much more effort into understanding and addressing it. That could include researchers changing what they work on, people within AI companies pushing for precautions, and governments taking the issue more seriously. And some of those people could be very competent and effective in ways we haven’t anticipated.

The big caveat is that we need enough time for that response to matter. It’s possible that the evidence becomes compelling only quite close to the point where things are very dangerous. So I wouldn’t want to rely on people rising to the occasion as our whole strategy. But I also think it’s a mistake to extrapolate from the current level of concern and assume that’s all the effort humanity will ever bring to bear on the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says researchers, company employees, and governments might respond more effectively as risks become clearer, but does not say that individual or small-group efforts could provide hope if society as a whole fails to rise to the occasion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one reason for hope is that the world could put a lot more effort into this than it currently does. Right now, the number of people seriously working on how to keep very powerful AI systems under control is pretty small relative to how important the problem could be. So you don’t need to imagine everyone suddenly becoming unusually wise. Even a relatively small fraction of people taking the problem seriously could make a substantial difference.

And people can change what they’re doing quite quickly when they see a concrete problem. Researchers can switch their focus, governments can build capacity, and people inside AI companies can push for better safety practices. I wouldn’t want to count on all of that happening, or happening early enough. Some of the difficulty is that we might need to act before there’s an unmistakable warning.

But I think it’s a mistake to look at the current level of preparation and assume that’s the level of preparation we’ll have throughout. There are a lot of capable people who haven’t really engaged with this yet. That’s both concerning and a substantial source of hope.

r001.rationale: The response says a relatively small fraction of people taking AI safety seriously could make a substantial difference, even without everyone changing or society broadly rising to the occasion.
